item.title: Todaiji and the Great Buddha: Nara's Colossal Temple — Guide
item.description: Todaiji is the grandest of Nara’s temples and one of Japan’s most awe-inspiring sights: founded in 752 as the head of all provincial Buddhist temples, it houses the Daibutsu, a 15-metre seated bronze Great Buddha, one of the largest bronze statues in the world, enshrined within the Daibutsuden — for centuries the largest wooden building on earth. The approach passes through the towering Nandaimon gate, guarded by a pair of ferocious 8-metre Nio guardian statues carved in the 13th century, while sacred deer roam the grounds.

item.title: Nara Family Trip: Deer Park, Giant Buddha & Hands-On Craft Workshops
item.description: Nara delivers one of Japan’s most genuinely child-friendly travel experiences — not because it has been engineered for tourism, but because its main attraction (wild deer roaming freely through a park containing one of the world’s most impressive buildings) is inherently captivating for children at almost any age. Unlike Tokyo’s theme parks, there’s nothing manufactured here. The deer are real, the Buddha is genuinely enormous, and the pillar hole children crawl through is 1,300 years old.

item.title: Top Sightseeing in Nara: Todai-ji, Kasuga Taisha & the Sacred Deer Park
item.description: Nara was Japan’s first permanent capital (710–784 AD), and the density of world-class heritage packed into one small city is extraordinary: a UNESCO-listed primeval forest, the world’s largest wooden building, Japan’s oldest wooden structures, and some 1,200 free-roaming sacred deer. Unlike Kyoto, most of Nara’s major sights sit within easy walking distance of each other — and the relative lack of international mass tourism means you can still find pockets of genuine stillness even at popular sites if you time your visit correctly.
